title: Georgia Works to Rebuild Trust in Its Elections
summary:
In a warehouse in Paulding County, Georgia, workers are unpacking voting machines and testing them for logic and accuracy. The checks are part of a statewide routine as Georgia prepares for midterm elections next month, to make sure every vote is counted correctly.

Ballot scanners, made by Dominion Voting Systems, are each locked in six different places to stop tampering. Lacy Dunn, the assistant elections director in Paulding County, says workers test every race, every candidate, every piece of equipment, and every ballot.

Brad Raffensperger, Georgia's secretary of state for the past eight years, oversees the work and stays in daily contact with all 159 counties. Georgia has been at the center of a national debate since President Donald Trump made false claims about its role in the 2020 election, and Raffensperger refused to help overturn that result. In January, FBI agents searched the Fulton County election headquarters and took hundreds of boxes of 2020 election material; almost nine months later, no charges have been brought. Some voters are unsure, while others feel hopeful their vote will be counted.
why_it_matters: When you grow up and vote, you will want to know that your vote is counted correctly, just like the voters in this story.

background_read: In an election, voters choose leaders by marking ballots, and machines help count those ballots.
Before voting day, election workers test the machines again and again to make sure every choice is counted correctly.
These checks matter because people need to trust that the final count truly shows what voters decided.
